findings.title: Related or rogue recipient keys turn the public epoch chain into a decryption of M (no proof of possession anywhere)
findings.detail: Multi-recipient ElGamal with one shared r is insecure when an adversary can register a key that is an affine function of an honest recipient's key. For any two recipients with A_j = t*A_i + x*B and known (t != 1, x): c_j - t*c_i - x*E = (1-t)*M, so M and DEK = KDF(M) follow from public data alone. Concrete instances: (a) register -A_i (flip bit 255 of Alice's 64-hex endpoint id; iroh::EndpointId, VerifyingKey::from_bytes and the design's decode_point all accept it: canonical and torsion-free), then c_i + c_j = 2M; (b) register 2*A_i, then 2c_i - c_j = M; (c) register the identity point (0x01,0,...,0), which iroh accepts and decode_point passes (is_torsion_free(O) is true; section 8 rejects E=O and c_i=O but never A_i=O), then c_j = M verbatim. In every case the DLEQ verifies, dek_commit matches, every honest reader decrypts correctly, and nothing in section 8 fires; all that is needed is one legitimate admin granting read to the rogue 'identity' (an ordinary add-reader epoch). Who can mount it: whoever registers identities (service admin, or a DB writer) — in E2E mode exactly the operator the mode claims cannot read — and because the leak needs no private key, every replica, every reader and anyone holding a stolen SQLite copy gets M too. The X25519-compat mode makes a +-A pair reachable by accident (the compat lift of a reader's own derived age recipient is +-A of its Ed25519 key), and the design never defines which of A+/-A+ is a compat recipient's id. Today's age wraps have no such property (the DH output is hashed per recipient), so this is a regression introduced by the algebraic wrap; the BBS insider-security theorem cited in 9.4 assumes honestly generated keys and the design silently drops that assumption.
findings.fix: (1) Verifier: reject any recipient set containing both P and -P (two ids differing only in bit 255) and any small-order recipient including the identity (add !A.is_small_order() to decode_point for keys) — closes only the cheap +-A/O class. (2) Proof of possession: the first epoch in which a recipient key appears in a chain carries a 64-byte Ed25519 signature by that key over "secret-bunker-epoch/1 pop" || 0x00 || group_id || key, verified by every verifier; AddIdentity requires the same PoP (or must arrive over a connection authenticated as that key); pinned keys deliver PoP at CreateGroup/migration, X25519-compat pinned keys sign with the clamped scalar. Knowledge of the secret key is exactly the model under which shared-randomness ElGamal is secure against related keys.

findings.title: The verifier never forces a generation bump when a reader is removed: 'kick' without 'roll' verifies
findings.detail: Rule 3 requires recipients(wraps) == readers(acl) ∪ pinned; rule 12 allows dek_version == head.dek_version provided dek_commit == head.dek_commit. An epoch that drops reader Bob from the ACL, keeps dek_version, and carries a fresh wrap set for the SAME M to the reduced recipient set satisfies both (fresh r, valid proof, identical commit). Bob keeps M and therefore the DEK under which every future write lands; server and replicas accept. Today store::revoke_read_and_rotate makes 'revocation rotates' a transactional invariant; in the design it is client-side procedure (12.3) with no verifier rule. The user's ask is 'kick out other users and roll the key'; the verifier enforces only the first half.
findings.fix: Add a verifier rule between steps 12 and 13: if (readers(head.acl) ∪ head.pinned) is not a subset of (readers(acl) ∪ pinned) then dek_version must equal head.dek_version + 1 and reencrypted must be non-zero. One set comparison over already-decoded data.

findings.title: Step 7 checks the NEW ACL, so an admin without read can author a garbage rotation that wipes the group
findings.detail: Step 7 requires author ∈ readers(acl) ∪ pinned of the record itself. An admin holding only the admin bit adds itself as a reader in the same epoch, bumps dek_version, wraps a fresh M it chose, commits honestly, and uploads garbage or empty re-encrypted versions with a matching reencrypted digest. Everything in section 8 passes; the server applies epoch + versions + pruning in one transaction (12.3); every reader then fails AEAD on every version and the data is gone unless there is an external backup. 12.1 says 'An admin without read cannot rotate (no M)', which is the intent but not what the rule checks. Today a non-reader admin's RotateDek re-encrypts nothing and grant-read needs the operational key, so no equivalent wipe exists.
findings.fix: When key material moves (dek_version changes or any recipient is added), additionally require author ∈ readers(head.acl) ∪ head.pinned — the previous epoch. Default open question 4 to retaining the previous generation's ciphertexts and wrap set for a grace window so a garbage rotation is recoverable by any previous reader without the backup key. In server-recipient mode the server is a recipient of both generations: decrypt old and new ciphertext for every version and refuse the commit on mismatch or AEAD failure.

findings.title: 'A compromised authoritative node degrades to withholding' is false in both deployment modes
findings.detail: (a) Server-recipient mode: the operational Ed25519 key is pinned and step 13 authorizes any pinned key to author any epoch ('the only party that can always author an epoch'). A compromised node holds that key online, so it can mint an epoch adding itself or anyone as reader and kicking every admin, with a valid proof and signature every replica accepts — exactly the forgery 12.4 lists as 'gained' protection. (b) E2E mode: the body carries keys, not names, and the admin client resolves names to endpoint ids through the node (Grant takes a name today; ListIdentityNames/ListIdentities are the only resolvers). A compromised node answers 'bob = A_srv' and the admin signs an add-reader epoch that hands M to the node. (c) Replicas: genesis is TOFU (12.2) and groups absent from the manifest are dropped (sync-protocol §8); drop 'prod', re-present it with a fresh chain (attacker ACL, attacker ciphertexts, attacker-authored epoch 1); the replica accepts the new genesis and the k8s operator renders attacker-chosen Secrets.
findings.fix: Split 'pinned' into recipient-only (operational key: wrapped to, never authors) and recovery (backup key: may author). Server-driven kicks in server-recipient mode are authored and signed by the requesting service admin's own client key; the node only verifies, stores and relays, and holds no epoch-authoring key. For (b) the admin client verifies endpoint ids out of band (fingerprint confirmation) or consumes a service-admin-signed identity registry; note the PoP of finding 1 does not fix substitution of the attacker's own key. For (c) replicas persist genesis hash per group name and treat a different genesis for a known name as an alarm requiring operator action, never an automatic re-TOFU.

findings.title: Re-encryption on rotation is an unauthenticated plaintext-rewrite channel attributed to the original writer
findings.detail: The rotating author decrypts every retained version and re-encrypts it; the verifier checks only that the reencrypted digest equals SHA-256 over the uploaded (name, version, dek_version, nonce, H(ciphertext)) list. Nothing binds the new ciphertext's plaintext to the old one. An admin-reader without the write bit (or a compromised admin key) can substitute the plaintext of any version while version numbers and created_by stay as they were; the only signed artefact says 'X re-encrypted', not 'X changed the content'. In E2E mode no verifier can detect it; in server-recipient mode the server could compare plaintexts but the design does not say it does. Today a rewrite is a Put with created_by = the rewriter, so this weakens the audit story the user explicitly asked for.
findings.fix: Carry a per-version plaintext commitment that survives rotation and is checked by readers after decryption: at Put the writer signs "secret-bunker-put/1" || 0x00 || group_id || u64be(len(name)) || name || u64be(version) || SHA-256(salt || plaintext) with its endpoint key, salt being 32 stored random bytes (stops dictionary attacks on low-entropy secrets); store (salt, writer, sig) in secret_version, include them in the reencrypted digest so the epoch signature binds them, copy them verbatim on rotation, and treat a post-decrypt signature failure as the same attributable alarm as a dek_commit mismatch. Server-recipient mode additionally compares plaintexts before commit.

findings.title: r-freshness (rule R1) is a prover-side MUST with no verifier check, although reuse is publicly detectable
findings.detail: Reusing r across generations gives a kicked reader holding M_old the value M_new = M_old + (c_i' - c_i): the rotation is void against precisely the adversary it exists for. A buggy client (seed-derived r, cloned VM, test hook left on) produces this silently. Since E = r*B, reuse is visible: two epochs with equal eph have equal r.
findings.fix: Verifier rejects an epoch whose eph equals the eph of any earlier epoch in the chain (index group_epoch on (group_id, eph); at minimum compare with head). Also mix chain position into r's derivation (r = H(OsRng 64 || group_id || dek_version || prev)) so a repeated RNG state still yields distinct r.

findings.title: A 'rotation' that keeps M is undetectable by keyless verifiers and unchecked by readers
findings.detail: Bump dek_version to v+1 but wrap the old M, committing honestly to KDF(M_old, group_id, v+1): proof, commit and re-encryption all verify, yet a kicked reader holding M_old computes DEK_{v+1} = KDF(M_old, group_id, v+1) and reads everything written afterwards. The verifier cannot know M changed (9.3.1), but readers hold M_old and can.
findings.fix: Reader step 6 gains: if dek_version increased, compare the recovered M' with the previous generation's M in constant time; equality is an alarm attributable to author. It also catches an honest client that forgot to draw a fresh m.

findings.title: Ed25519 acceptance criteria are implementation-dependent; a malicious author can split the chain view between Rust and Go verifiers
findings.detail: Rust uses verify_strict (rejects small-order R and A, non-canonical S, non-canonical R via byte comparison). Go's ed25519.Verify rejects non-canonical S but accepts small-order R and A. A malicious author can craft a signature with a small-order R that Go accepts and Rust rejects; a Go replica fed by a malicious node accepts an epoch the Rust server never stored. The design pins verify_strict for Rust and says nothing for the Go client the brief says must keep working.
findings.fix: Specify the criteria normatively (author key via decode_point; R canonical bytes and not small order; S < l; non-cofactored equation), ship rejected-class vectors (small-order R, S+l, non-canonical R) in the cross-implementation test set, and have the Go client pre-check R (decode, 8*R == O, re-encode compare) before ed25519.Verify.

findings.title: group_id uniqueness is unenforced, so the KDF transplant-resistance claim in section 3 rests on nothing
findings.detail: group_id is chosen by whoever mints epoch 1 (a client); 12.5 adds secret_group.group_id_bytes without a UNIQUE constraint. Two groups with equal group_id and dek_version derive the same DEK from the same M, so a wrap set can be carried between them by an admin of both. No leak in itself, but section 3's 'a wrap set can never be transplanted between groups or generations even if the proof check were skipped' is only true if group_ids are distinct.
findings.fix: UNIQUE(group_id_bytes) on secret_group; CreateGroup/SubmitEpoch rejects a genesis whose group_id already exists; replicas key their chain store on group_id as well as name.

strengths: decode_point is exactly right against curve25519-dalek 5.0.0: decompress does not check y < p or the x=0/sign-bit case, and recompress-and-compare plus the exact l*P == O check closes every non-canonical and torsion input; the 'reject, never clear' rationale (readers decrypt in E, not E/E[8]) is correct.

The batched Sigma-protocol with a shared witness is sound: special soundness extracts one r satisfying all n relations from two transcripts with equal commitments, and the e-form means commitments are never transmitted, so torsion cannot enter through R_i.

Strong Fiat-Shamir over the full statement (domain, group_id, dek_version, dek_commit, n, E, every A_i and c_i in sorted order, all fixed-width) binds the proof to exactly the bases and ciphertexts the verifier uses; Delta-shift and swap attacks are correctly excluded.

Reader decryption with SigningKey::to_scalar (verified in ed25519-dalek 3.0.0: clamp then from_bytes_mod_order) is exact on a torsion-free E; the design correctly identifies why torsion in E would make two correct implementations disagree.

The signature domain prefix is verified not to collide with anything iroh signs under the same key (TLS CertificateVerify begins with 64 spaces; iroh-relay signs 16/32 pseudorandom bytes; pkarr begins with bencode), and verify_strict plus decode_point on the author key yields the strict variant.

HKDF split of DEK and dek_commit from one PRK with (group_id, dek_version) in info is a clean binding commitment whose disclosure reveals nothing about the DEK, and the reader-side constant-time commit check turns 'same M for everyone' into 'same M and the committed one'.
verdict: The proof, encoding and transcript layer is sound as specified, and its library-level claims check out against the pinned crate sources. The design fails at the boundary where the algebraic wrap meets adversarially chosen keys — with no proof of possession, related keys (−A, 2A, the identity) make M computable from the public chain by anyone, a regression from age wraps that voids the E2E-mode confidentiality claim — and at verifier rules that do not enforce what the prose promises: removal of a reader does not force a generation bump, step 7 tests the wrong ACL, the pinned operational key lets a compromised node author any epoch, and re-encryption is an unsigned content-rewrite channel. Not shippable until findings 1–5 are folded into sections 8 and 12; the minor findings are cheap hardening.
